To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Symbiodinium are present in all 39 scleractinians species tested; 2) all 26 symbiotic specialists host two or more Symbiodinium; 3) on average, 2.2 Symbiodinium were found in each coral species; 4) the average number of Symbiodinium was significantly greater than one; and 5) all four Symbioidinium clades were present in 21 of the 39

1) Symbiodinium diversity within individual corals is greater than previously thought; 2) the ability to associate and host multiple symbiont types (i.e. ‘symbiotic flexibility’) is common in sclerotinian corals and 3) the potential for corals to respond to climate change via shifts in their symbiont communities may be more widespread than previously assumed.

the capacity to associate with multiple algal symbionts is common in sclercatinian (stony corals), and that the potential for reef coral to acclimate or adapt to environmental stressors via symbiont shifts may therefore be phylogenetically widespread.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between corals and the algae they live with.
the relationship between corals and their symbiotic algae.
the symbiosis between coral polyps and photosynthetic algae (genus Symbioinium).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
coral symbioses are not specific, and that specificity is relative.
‘specificity’ in coral–Symbiodinium symbioses is rare.
coral species are not ‘specific’ for any one symbiont clade and, therefore, are not ‘specialists’.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
coral species that are considered to be symbiotic specialists are not as specific as previously thought and that they are likely to have more flexibility than previously thought.
the ability to switch symbiont clade is common in sclercatinian corals and that the potential for reef coral to adapt to climate change may therefore be widespread than has previously assumed.
coral–algal associations are highly dynamic, and that corals are likely to be able to respond to climate change via shifts in symbiont community composition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
coral–Symbiodinium specificity may be more flexible than we previously thought.
coral–algal associations are not as specific as we once thought.
coral–algal specificity is not absolute.
